utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If there are no procedural matters to be raised, we'll move -- and it appears that there are none, we'll move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in closed session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness DST-074.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration you've given yesterday is still binding upon you. That is, that you should speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Bakrac will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone in the courtroom and around the courtroom. Good morning, Mr. DST-074. I would like to show you another clip. I would like to see whether you recognise anybody in the clip. In your statement you said something about the event, so let's see whether the clip reflects what you stated in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My assistant is going to play 2D877 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the two individuals in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who are they?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: The first one, or the one on the left, is Stojcic, and next to him in the distance is Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say Stojcic, you mean Badza?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we continue, please -- or, rather, can we stop here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a board that you can see in the background. Do you recognise the board and the place? Do you know that this is the training centre in Erdut where you say you were billeted together with the rest of your men?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the board that was displayed at that centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, but it seems to me that it would be helpful to have time codes on the record so we know what the witness is referring to at each point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac, that came to my mind as well. When you stopped for the first time, at what time code was that in this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I understood you properly, the clip, or that episode, starts at 11:30. 11 minutes, 30 seconds. I apologise, 11:20 I have just been suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then briefly go back to the picture on which the witness commented so that we can identify it with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'm going to ask my colleague to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The two persons you asked the witness questions about, which he identified as Badza and Arkan, were shown at 11:26 in this clip. Please proceed now to 11:31, because that's, I think, where we saw the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, the board that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we now move to 11:31. We can play it until it's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are now at 11:31, and that's the board you asked questions about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, this is the board in front of which the two persons were standing. Does it say here that this is the training centre for volunteers and the TO of the Serbian provinces of Slavonia, Baranja, Srem and Erdut.

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says on the board.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the area? Do you recognise the board? Was the clip taken in the centre where you were also billeted?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw the board already there when we arrived at Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm kindly asking the assistant to proceed for another 20 or 30 seconds, and that will be the end of that clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, I've asked you to look at the clip. I have only two or three more questions. In the background we saw some military vehicles. At the time when you were there, did Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, have any military vehicles or tanks?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was there, there was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We also saw soldiers in training. We saw them wearing overalls. Are those just regular overalls or NATO overalls?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were regular overalls. However, Zeljko Raznjatovic and his group of men who were billeted in Erdut when we arrived there, they wore NATO uniforms, and they were two-piece uniforms, not overalls.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what about their weapons, the weapons that the persons in training at the centre carried, were those any special weapons?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could notice, in most cases those were automatic rifles of local-made. And I also saw Skorpios being carried by a few people, or pistols that the army used to have. The police and the MUP did not have those weapons as a standard issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just two more questions, Your Honours. We said that we would provide Mr. Farr with the DVD, and we will subsequently tender the video-clip for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'm a bit confused by the last few questions. A comparison is made to what you see on the screen and what others may have worn at any time, because the group or the members of this group are not identified as such. Now, half of the answers is that this is not the type of uniform, the gear, that Arkan and his people had, and in other parts of the answer a comparison is made with the MUP, the ordinary. So I'm a bit confused. Apparently this is not the gear that you would see when Arkan was there, which suggests - but I do not know whether you or the witness would have any further information - that this is not Arkan's Men. The second is that this is not the type of uniforms or gear that -- or the weaponry that the MUP would have. So it's neither Arkan's people or MUP people, which have -- has not identified it. But on the basis of the weapons, it could not be MUP; on the basis of the gear, it could not be Arkan. That's at least what is suggested in the answer. I'm a bit lost there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. If I may be of assistance and clarify some things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When it comes to the overalls and the area where those men carried out their training, that is the centre in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: This clip was taken at a time when I was not present in Erdut. This could have been either in late 1991 or 1992 and further on. Zeljko Raznjatovic conducted training at that centre when we left. I know that he had tanks and all the other weapons. At one point in time, the person who committed crimes in the municipality of Becej where I was chief, he broke into a church and took some icons. That person was billeted at the centre. And Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan -- upon my assistance, I came to the centre, and Zeljko Raznjatovic handed over that person. That's why I recognise the uniforms worn by the men who were in training under him. They were members of that anti-armour platoon or unit, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you recognise the picture where it was, the gate which was opened? Was that the Erdut centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see you're nodding in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That's at the centre of Erdut. If you go towards the winery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The winery is right at the centre, and in the background you see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... yes, it's fine. You affirmed that this is -- these are pictures taken in the Erdut centre. Mr. Bakrac, no further questions? Or do you have more questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, just two more brief questions and I'll be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, you said you were present at the ceremony at Kula in 1997.

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you see Arkan at Kula at that time?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. And one last question, witness. In your statement, you mentioned a person known as Beli. You said you turned him back from the check-point, from the crossing. Who was that person with the nickname Beli?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I said all I knew in my statement, and I repeated it several times. I did not know Belgrade and Belgrade criminals so that not a single name meant anything to me. Giska, Arkan, Beli; those names meant nothing to me. They were the same to me as criminals in my own area that broke into kiosks. The first group of armed men who came to my check-point wishing to cross over were they. I don't remember the exact date, but two bus-loads of them came. They were equipped and armed. And they had been engaged by the Serbian Revival Movement and there occurred a clash. I even put a bullet in my rifle and I was ready to fire to save my own men. However, Goran Hadzic came and said that they did not need volunteers. But there was a man from Trpinje, nicknamed Tasak, who started making a lot of trouble. I can't remember his actual name but if somebody said it to me, I would be able to recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You asked who a person was with the nickname Beli. The witness tells us all kind of things which seems not to focus very much on your question. Could you please tell us: Who was the person with the nickname Beli? Without describing all kind of events and whether you used your weaponry, or ... just that person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the man who brought that group of 40 to 60 armed men. That same evening, that gentleman was killed and I was one of the suspects in that killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, was Beli at the head of a group that had a certain name?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the group that the Serbian Revival Movement set up, trained, and wanted to send over the border. I can't remember whether they were called the Serb Volunteer Guard or something. Zeljko Raznjatovic's unit and that other unit had similar names. I think it's Serbian Volunteer Guard. All I know is that they were members of the SPO, Serbian Revival Movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I may jog your memory, would you agree that he headed a unit, a paramilitary unit that was called the Serbian Guard?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's right. And later he was replaced by Giska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honours. Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Farr, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness DST-074, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Farr. Mr. Farr is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Good afternoon -- good morning, DST-074. Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. And I can see you very well. Thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear that. We have a lot of material, and I'm going to try to focus my questions as specifically as possible. And I would ask you to listen to the question and try to focus your answer as specifically as possible as well. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope I have done that so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd like to start by asking you about the provincial SUP of Vojvodina and the MUP the Serbia. In your statement and your evidence yesterday, you mentioned both of those institutions, the provincial SUP of Vojvodina and the MUP the Serbia, and you indicated that they were independent. But despite this independence the SUP of Vojvodina and the MUP of Serbia co-operated, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: All the SUPs of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia co-operated among themselves, including Vojvodina, Serbia, Kosovo, Slovenia, and everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And there are actually some examples of that co-operation in your statement, I think, and I'm going to ask you whether you agree. The deployment of your PJM unit to Belgrade during the 9 March 1991 demonstrations; that's an example of co-operation between the Vojvodina provincial SUP and the MUP of Serbia. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that. And that was always with the approval of the federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And related to that event: When Jovica Stanisic met with the commander of your unit at that time; that's also an example of that kind of co-ordination between the provincial SUP and -- of Vojvodina and the Serbian MUP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Because I was on assignment to provide security to the president and his residence, and Mr. Jovica Stanisic was on the same assignment, which means we were doing the same job. Everyone in -- in his -- each in his own line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Right. And with respect to lines of work, that meeting between Jovica Stanisic and your unit commander is actually an example of co-ordination between the DB of the Serbian MUP and the public security service of the Vojvodina provincial SUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Since we didn't know Belgrade that well, that was an assignment we had just received one or two days before. It's normal we had to get to know things before we were able to complete the assignment successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: The fact that you were ordered to accept permits assigned by Radmilo Bogdanovic when you were stationed at the crossing at Vajska; that is also an example of co-ordination between the provincial SUP of Vojvodina, you and Zavisic, and the MUP of Serbia, Bogdanovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. First I was told that Mr. Markov, the provincial secretary, was also able to sign such permits. And after that, I was told that the permits were valid with the signature of Radmilo Bogdanovic, who was at the head of the federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And you were told that by your superior, Miodrag Zavisic, who, like you, was in the Vojvodina provincial SUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: We received that order at Odzaci, as I said yesterday, by chief of the provincial SUP, Marinko Kresoja, Momo Stojanovic, and Stanoje Milanovic. One of these three told us this, I don't know which one. But Zavisic was designated as man number one to whom we would report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In addition, the fact that the group that went to Eastern Slavonia to set up the TO staff was composed of officers from the provincial SUP of Vojvodina, as well as 16 members of the special police unit from Belgrade; that's another example of co-operation between the Vojvodina provincial SUP and the Serbian MUP. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. That is not co-operation. We went over as volunteers. We all signed statements that we were volunteers. We were rallied by Stojcic, Badza, but Zavisic first. But several times before, Goran Hadzic and the others had insisted that I should transfer, and I said I was not able to because I had a full-time job. However, when Zavisic asked me to join the volunteers, I agreed. I crossed over of my own will. I signed a statement that I was a volunteer. And I was no longer a member of the force, apart from the fact that I received my salary at my police station where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Is it correct that the members of the special police force from Belgrade were normally part of the Serbian MUP, before they volunteered?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Before that, they had their jobs in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And at the time that you volunteered, was Badza associated with the Serbian MUP or the Vojvodina SUP?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Badza was linked to the SUP of Serbia, not Vojvodina. We met up quite often in the area of Kosovo, and that's where I know him from.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And the other four officers who went to Eastern Slavonia, that's yourself, Trajkovic, and two people whose names I can't remember at the moment, were associated with the Vojvodina SUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. Badza, Trajkovic, and Simovic were all from Belgrade; while Zavisic and I were natives of Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So the group that went to Eastern Slavonia to set up the TO staff consisted of people whose regular employment posts were with both the Serbian MUP and the Vojvodina SUP?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Before that, Zavisic and I worked in the MUP of Vojvodina; whereas the other group used to work in Serbia. The TO staff existed even before we arrived in Western Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem. We didn't set it up. We just continued to work there on assignments received from Goran Hadzic. But the rest of the time I saw very little of Goran, and we received all our further assignments from Mr. Stojcic, nicknamed Badza.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And you all continued to be paid by the Serbian MUP or the Vojvodina SUP respectively; correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about them. I know that I received my salary at the OUP Becej.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. I would now like --

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: And every month - excuse me - every month, I had to send a certificate in order to be able to receive the salary that Badza had to approve in the -- in the area of Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. I want to make sure that I understand the dates that -- that we're dealing with in your statement and evidence. You said you arrived in Vajska on approximately the 15th of May, 1991, and you stayed until a few days after Dalj fell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th, if memory serves me well, I arrived at Vajska and a couple of days after the fall of Dalj and when the bridge was liberated. I know Zavisic asked me and it took a couple of days of consultations before I agreed and before we crossed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So you arrived at Vajska on the 13th of May, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And you left a few days after -- you went to Eastern Slavonia a few days after Dalj fell, on the 1st or 2nd of August, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'll repeat. You went to Eastern Slavonia a few days after Dalj fell, and Dalj fell on the 1st or 2nd of August, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And you remained in Eastern Slavonia for approximately two months, which by my calculation would be late September or early October; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: The date when I returned I can determine by the wounded -- wounding of Ilija Kojic, when they moved towards Bogdanovci. It was five or six days after he was wounded that I returned. I don't know the exact date. Because I had a lot of trouble getting that information because I had left the ministry. And when I asked for my daily reports that I had written every day, were difficult to get, inaccessible to me. So you have to excuse me if I'm off by a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I now have a few questions about the procedures at Vajska crossing and your job related to preventing the illegal transport of weapons. As I understand your evidence, you said that, in general, you checked people for weapons, you didn't allow anyone with weapons to cross unless they had a permit from Bogdanovic or Markov, you seized the weapons of anyone who tried to cross the border with a weapon, and you seized a lot of weapons in that process. Is that an accurate summary?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that the task of preventing illegal crossings with weapons was a very difficult task for which you and the other members of the PJM did not have enough men and did not have all of the right equipment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And while you did your best to stop it, if someone was determined to cross the Danube illegally with weapons, they probably would be able to do it, not at a check-point but somewhere; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: At the check-point, they would cross only over my dead body. As for other places, to the extent that I had resources and to the extent I knew where they would be attempting to cross, I tried to cover the area 24 hours/7.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You did your best, but you allow for the possibility that there could have been illegal crossings, despite your best efforts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: The Danube river is winding and very long, and I suppose that's a possibility. But I tried to minimise that possibility with the men that I led and in direct co-operation with the residents of that area. And in that area there were many farms and fields, and I made contact with all these people and in a way they cooperated with me because there were Serbs, Croats, and Hungarians living there whose interests were the same as mine, namely to minimise the number of armed men in that area, first of all, for their own safety, and then for ours too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: When individuals were crossing at Vajska, you would check the identifications of everyone except for military people because you weren't authorised to request military IDs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at everybody's papers, including those of military personnel. A military person had to show ID, otherwise they would not be able to cross. Because anybody could have put on a military uniform. Only people with proper military ID were able to cross. Those who didn't produce one were turned back. I would call the secretariat in charge, or the military police, and that person would be taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In paragraph 45 of your statement, it says: "Members of the military intelligence service were also crossing the check-point. They represented themselves like that, but I did not ask them to legitimise themselves because I was not entitled to request for military ID cards." Do you have a correction to that?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I meant, they did not -- I did not search them when they produced the military ID. It was a small number of military personnel that crossed over at that point. Those were individual cases. They had to show ID, but I did not search them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Does that include members of the military intelligence service? You would check their IDs as well?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: A group of men from the military security did come. They were very polite. They produced their IDs of their own will. They did not ask to cross the border. They just wanted information. And we treated them the same as employees of the state security. Every time they would arrive at the crossing, we would make an Official Note, and in most cases it was I who spoke to them, and every time a report would be written about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Were identifications provided by the Vojvodina provincial SUP and the Serbian MUP the same or different?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: They were very similar. They were all blue. The writing said "Official ID." The one from Vojvodina bore the coat of arms of Vojvodina. The Serbian one bore the coat of arms of Serbia. But the Vojvodina one was multi-lingual because it was in Hungarian and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did everyone who crossed the border need a permit to cross, or only people who wanted to cross with weapons?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Only people who wanted to cross with weapons. The locals from Croatia would just have to produce their personal ID. People who had IDs from Serbia or Vojvodina had to produce a certificate from the TO in Vajska and other places. These TO staffs would issue permits for individual crossings by regular citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You talked about seizing weapons. Would you seize the weapons only of people who wanted to cross the border, or would you seize the weapon of anyone who came to your check-point with a weapon?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: We not only seized weapons from people who tried to cross but we seized them from houses and estates in the broader area, acting on any report from Backa Palanka, Vajska, Glodjane. Any time we received a report, we would write it down, and we seized all the weapons we knew about, together with the local SUP. I think I've said that in my statement. I forwarded one such report and Glusica kind of cheated me and I lost an informant whom I had placed in that area, so I had lost an important source of information about where weapons could be found. Because the regular people, the local people, viewed us as a special unit. They never saw us in those uniforms of the regular force. It was a time when new uniforms were issued to the PJP. So the people saw us as a special unit who was able to do much more than we were actually able to, and we enjoyed the trust of the regular citizenry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, I appreciate the completeness of that answer, but this is actually an example of what I brought up at the beginning of my examination. My question was: Would you seize the weapon of anyone who came to your check-point with a weapon. And I think you answered that, but you also provided a lot of additional information. The problem is we have time constraints. So if you wouldn't mind, could I ask you to focus very specifically on my questions. My next question is: Yesterday, in your evidence, you said part of your job was to remove people who were in possession of weapons illegally and legally. Is it correct that you would seize weapons that were legally owned as well as those that were illegally owned?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, licences to carry weapons enabled people to carry weapons in any republic with such licence. After I arrived in Vajska, we seized weapons even from people who had such licences. And we took such people to the SUP where they would be interviewed. And in those interviews, the people were told that the licences would be taken away from them if they appeared in that area carrying that weapon, licence included. I'm sorry if I take too long in my answers, but if you want me to really say something meaningful, I have to, to provide such answers. I'm sorry if it's taking your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave it to Mr. Farr whether he considers short answers sufficient. And what is meaningful or not is primarily for Mr. Farr to decide. If any questions remain, we'll put them to you. The simple answer to the last question would have been: Yes, you would seize even weapons that were legally owned. If Mr. Farr needs further details, he'll ask you about it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In paragraph 20 of your statement, you said that Goran Hadzic and Ilija Kojic crossed the border at Vajska and you made a point of talking to them to gather information because you considered them to have more reliable information than other people. What was Goran Hadzic's position -- what did you understand Goran Hadzic's position to be at the time that you were at Vajska?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: My arrival at -- in Vajska was a matter of some confusion because within a very short period of time I received a lot of contradictory information. I did not filter it. I would just write all that information up and forward it. With time, I realized that Ilija Kojic and Goran Hadzic and some other people provided more accurate information. And every time they crossed, I would record it. And if there was time, I would talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I apologise for the interruption. We will -- we will get to those matters. But can we just start with the question of: What did you believe Goran Hadzic's position was when you were at Vajska?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija Kojic was commander of the TO, and Goran Hadzic was the president of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: How did you first meet Goran Hadzic and learn who he was?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: My first contact with him was when he crossed over by boat and when I asked for his ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And at that time did he tell you what his position was? In other words, did he introduce himself by his name and his position?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not introduce himself. He just showed me his ID. I recorded it. And I didn't even know what it was because I wanted, at that time, to talk to as many people as I could when they were crossing because I was gathering information. So we had this informal conversation. I wrote it up later in a note. A week or two later, the picture became clearer to me, and I began to have an idea how things were operating there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So why is it that you believed that Goran Hadzic had especially reliable information?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that. I said that happened in time. Ten, 15 days into my tour at this crossing, I realized Goran Hadzic had much more information than Kojic and many others, Lazic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name of all these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you learn what the source of Goran Hadzic's information was? Did he tell you how he knew certain things?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, the interpreters could not hear the names mentioned by the witness. You mentioned that Goran Hadzic had much more information than Kojic and many others, and then you mentioned, as the first one, Lazic. Who were the others you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vucenovic, Marko Loncarevic, and many others that I got to know later. The more time I spent at the check-point, the better picture I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: What kind of information was -- what kind of reliable information was Goran Hadzic able to provide to you?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, as soon as I arrived there was an incident -- there were incidents in which 250, 300 MUP members were killed, and into my stint, the number decreased, until there were 10, 11. So the information I got depended very much on who I got it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did Hadzic give you information about the security situation in Eastern Slavonia, for example?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the main thing, whether there were unrests, whether somebody was disturbing them, whether there were large crossings by groups, how the people were organised, whether there were village guards, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you ever learn why he was able to gather more accurate information than anyone else, or than most other people?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was the political leader there. After the drowning of Mr. Soskocanin, he is the one who took over responsibility and led those people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So he had access to higher-level people than other people who were crossing your border did; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what higher-level people you mean. There were no higher-level people there. He was the highest level person.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: How often did Hadzic cross into Serbia or into Vojvodina from Croatia during the period you were stationed at Vajska?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice a week, on average. Sometimes it would be fewer sometimes; sometimes more times. But, on average, twice a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you know where he was going, either in Vojvodina or Serbia, when he crossed the border?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: In most instances he met with Bosko Parasevic [phoen], the president of the municipality of Odzak, Mile Novakovic from Backa Palanka. And they mostly discussed the transfer of humanitarian aid to the people there. I often received news about lorries with the humanitarian aid coming my way. I would then inspect them and let them cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And I assume you learned what he was doing based on what he told you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. On many occasions he met with those men at the crossing itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: When he crossed the border, was he accompanied by body-guards?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: He had his own vehicle, or I don't know whose vehicle it was, and the registration plates are in my statement. On most occasions, David Cesic and Milenko Dafinic were with him. Their respective nicknames are Ceso and Dafo, if that means anything to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did Hadzic and Kojic cross the border together or separately? You mentioned them together in your statement, but I don't know if that was just because you were discussing that topic or ...

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, they crossed separately. There were, however, occasions when they crossed together. I could say a lot more about the crossings and the dates if I had been provided my Official Notes that I kept every day at the crossings. But I was never given them. I don't know why. The situation would be much clearer to you and you would learn a lot more from my daily reports that were extensive and provided a lot of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: How often did Ilija Kojic cross the border during the period you were at Vajska?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as often as Mr. Goran.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can you estimate how often? Would it be once every two weeks, for example, once a week?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said that Goran went across twice a week, I would say that he crossed once a week, on average.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And you just indicated that at that time he was the commander of the TO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If -- he was in charge organising the Territorial Defence and the police across the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And what kind of especially reliable information was he able to provide?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, he told me how many attacks had happened at the settled areas or the check-points or the barricades that they had set up, whether there were any disturbances, whether fire was opened. This is the kind of information I wanted from him, and I believe that I was provided that information. I really don't know whether that information was accurate and adequate. But whatever I heard from him, I noted in my reports. Whenever he crossed, he always pleaded for weapons from me. However, I was in no position to help him with that. I just couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: But he was eager to acquire weapons at that time?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked me for weapons. I don't know whether he obtained them. He never carried any weapons across the border. Even his personal weapons, he never had those on him because I wouldn't allow him to take them across.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, sir, just for the sake of clarity: You've said "he asked me for weapons." You're referring to Ilija Kojic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In paragraph 21 of your statement, you say that you never came across Ilija Kojic being involved in supplying weapons but you can't exclude the possibility that he was involved in that without your knowledge. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. At the crossings which I controlled, Ilija Kojic never transported a single rifle, a single round, a single bullet, anything. He didn't even transport a part of a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In paragraph 29 of your statement, you mention that Seselj also crossed the river at the Vajska check-point. Approximately how often or how many times did he cross during your time there?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: You will see it in the statement that it was three times. Once, he attended Soskocanin's funeral, and then once again after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: On the occasions other than Soskocanin's funeral, do you know why he was going to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time he crossed he contacted a man who was the president of his party in that area. He was a member of the Ministry of Information. His name is in my statement. Memory fails me at the moment. When I crossed over, he came to see me quite a number of times. He wanted me to help him, an article about the situation in the region. I know the name of the place, but I just can't remember it at the moment. He was the president of the party, and Seselj visited him to discuss the setting up of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did Seselj --

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Rade Leskovac. I apologise, Rade Leskovac is his name. I have to appreciate that everything happened quite a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Of course, of course. We understand that. Did Seselj provide you information in the same way that Kojic or Hadzic did?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't request information from Seselj about the situation in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you request or receive any other kind of information from Seselj?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He was very polite at the crossings. He was in possession of all the required documents. I didn't have much time to engage in a discussion with him, because at the time when he was crossing, another type of crossing had been set up involving a barge. So I really did not have much time to talk to him. The crossings were crowded. I didn't have time. I mostly talked to the people who were there waiting to cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you request or receive any other kind of information from Seselj? The simple answer is no. And then you start explaining that there was no time, that there were other ways of crossing. The simple answer -- if Mr. Farr wants to know why you did, he'll ask you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: All right. Turning to the permits to cross the border with weapons. In paragraph 32 of your statement, you said only people with a permit from the highest level would be allowed to cross the border with a weapon. And then you clarified that that meant either a permit signed by Bogdanovic or by Predrag Markov. That means that in your view Bogdanovic was someone with a high level of authority or, in fact, from the highest level in July of 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And I think we've already clarified this, but just to make it completely clear: That means that you as a member of the Vojvodina provincial SUP had been ordered to accept a permit issued by someone from the MUP of the Republic of Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, in fact, the only two people that you're aware of who crossed at your check-point with weapons, that is, Arkan and Rade Kostic, both had permits issued by Bogdanovic of the Serbian MUP rather than Markov of the Vojvodina SUP. That's also correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on to Arkan's attempts to cross the border and then subsequently crossing the border. The first time Arkan came to the border, when you turned him away, how many men and how many vehicles did he come with?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: It was around 1900 hours in the evening. He arrived with seven or eight men and with three or four jeeps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, I urged Mr. Jordash not to ask questions where the answers are easily found. I mean, we have the three jeeps in paragraph 34, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You're correct. I should have limited my question to the number of men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, then, of course, you would -- you might want to know whether -- I mean, three jeeps, load them very well, you have 15 to 20, and if you have less passengers then perhaps you have eight to 12. If it's of vital importance for you to know whether it was 8, 9, 12, 13, or 14, then of course ask your questions. If it's not really important, the picture is clear. He arrived with a couple of jeeps, people manning those jeeps, and we now even know that, I think, there were Mitsubishi Pajeros, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so we get four mules, six mules? What do you think it was? Let's try to focus on the core.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do believe that the information is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's not ask -- let's not be repetitious. If there is any clue in there, go to that point as quickly as you can. I know that cross-examination is an art, but efficiency and artistic performance, you should strike a fair balance between that. I am usually more in favour of less artistic performance, at least in the courtroom. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, would it be okay if we took the break now, Your Honour, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's quarter past 10.00, so that would be -- usually we have a break after 75 minutes, Mr. Farr. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, you may proceed. And, as you know, proceeding means moving forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, before the break you told us that Arkan arrived with seven or eight men. How many men did you have with you at the check-point at that time?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Who was better armed, Arkan's eight men or your three men?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan's Men.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did they have permits for the modern Heckler weapons that you indicate they had with them?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: The permit listed all the weapons, we checked everything, and then they were let go. Everything tallied with the crossing permit - the names, the family names, and the registration numbers of the vehicles that were either in the cars or on the bodies of Arkan's group.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you recall whether their weapons permits had been issued by the Serbian MUP or the Vojvodina MUP?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: That permit was issued by the MUP of Serbia. It was signed by Radmilo Bogdanovic. That kind of weapons was not a standard issue in the MUP. Neither in the territory of Vojvodina or Serbia did I see that kind of weapons in the hands of MUP members, and with that I also mean Kosovo, where I did a number of tours. Moreover, my men, the members of my group, did not even know the proper name of that kind of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, you've just mentioned the permit signed by Bogdanovic that Arkan had the second day. On the first day, when he came to the border and asked to cross, did you check for weapon permits on that occasion, or no?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that meeting actually bordering on a conflict breaking out between me and my men, on the one hand, and him and his men, on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: But you didn't let him cross because you were determined to carry out your orders and respect the law; correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I disallowed that. However, when we left, I informed my superiors about his presence and about his conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: At page 73 of the transcript yesterday, you said that no one was able to control Arkan. In fact, you've just told us that you were able to stop Arkan and eight relatively heavily armed men with three of your men. Doesn't that show that someone with sufficient determination determines to enforce the law could stop Arkan?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that, I meant people from across the border. Once I crossed, I tried to act in a similar way, but Radovan Stojcic would not allow me to do that. Radovan Stojcic said that whatever problems that they had with him would be his responsibility, that he would deal with everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In other words, it's not that Arkan couldn't be controlled; it's that there was a decision taken not to control him.

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: No such decision was ever taken. For us to do anything, we had to have an approval. The 16 policemen that had crossed over, together with me, on several occasions attended meetings and asked to be transferred from Erdut and for Arkan to be removed. We wanted to leave the area. And Badza always claimed that he would deal with the matter and that he would make sure that Arkan behaved in accordance with the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, would you allow me to ask one clarifying question. We've heard Arkan arriving late at night with some men in the possession of weapons. You didn't know about Arkan. He said that he was sent by Bogdanovic. Now, you earlier told us that you would not allow anyone to cross without the required documents, but you also told us that anyone who was in possession of weapons, whether legally owned or not, you would seize them. Why didn't you seize the weapons of a man you were not familiar with as being Arkan on that same evening? Why didn't you seize the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had in mind the security of my people and my own security and safety. People who had arrived with him had already taken favourable positions, so both me and my men would have come under threat. Having known Arkan as he was -- actually, I only learned it subsequently. At that moment, I did not know who Arkan was. He was just an ordinary Joe like anyone else. However, if I had been in a position to do that, I would have done it, you -- you rest assured. I think that my move was smarter because I spared the lives of my men and my own life. I faltered a little when I heard him say that he had been sent by Mr. Bogdanovic. I hesitated but still did what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say people who had arrived with him had already taken favourable positions. What do you mean exactly by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he arrived and when he told me who he was and that he was there to cross, our conversation started calmly. However, when he realized that I was determined not to let him go, his men got out of the vehicles and took positions on the ground from which they could shoot. I did put a rifle -- a bullet in -- in -- in the barrel so I would have fought and I would have taken one of them with me, but I didn't think that that was necessary. I thought that there were ways to disarm him and his men. However, when he came back with the permit, there was no reason for me not to let him cross the river.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand your story well, you would not have stopped him if he would have wanted to cross. Sending him back was because he consented to that, rather than that you forced him to go back. Because you say: We couldn't take the weapons. They were ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He couldn't cross. In order to cross the Danube, he should have had a vehicle. I had already transferred the vehicle to the other bank. The person who was in charge of driving that, when things came to a head, I said to the men to cross the Danube. The only thing that could have happened was an incident and we would have killed each other. But you have to rest assured that he would not have crossed, even if that had taken my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you were unable to seize his weapons. He had better weapons. They were in the majority. That was the situation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's it. And after his voluntary action, he rallied his men back into the vehicle and returned, seeing that he couldn't accomplish his objective. The next day he was a different man, very courteous. He even apologised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You said that there was no way Arkan was going to cross without a permit. You've also said yesterday that Arkan couldn't be controlled. Isn't it correct that senior members of the MUP, and, in particular, Bogdanovic, could have prevented Arkan from crossing the border simply by not giving him a permit?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on people above me. All I know is what I did. I don't know what Radmilo Bogdanovic did. He did not account to me. I was passing on my information to Markov, my first superior, that is, Zavisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: But as far as you're concerned, you would never have let Arkan across the border without a permit from Bogdanovic or Markov?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. Either I or he. He couldn't cross with me on that check-point. But, rest assured that he wouldn't have crossed anyway without an appropriate permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Now, on the second occasion, the next morning, as we've been discussing, he had a permit signed by Bogdanovic. Do you know why he got a permit from Bogdanovic, who I assume was in Belgrade, rather than from Markov, who I assume was in Novi Sad? Isn't Novi Sad closer to where you are -- where you were than Belgrade is?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you mean Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about Arkan, the next morning.

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose. I can't be sure. But I believe that Arkan lived in Belgrade, and it was easier for him to get a permit there. Secondly, I believe that Markov didn't know Arkan either, and he wouldn't have given him one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So your assumption is that Arkan was closer to the Serbian MUP leadership than to the Vojvodina SUP leadership?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only guess based on the permit he brought, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's refrain from guessing or invitations to guess. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: The permit that Arkan showed you was the first permit you had seen for someone to cross the border with weapons. This was an extraordinary situation. You must have reviewed the permit very carefully; correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: He took it, compared everything, kept it, and forwarded it through me to Zavisic. Where he got it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You personally saw the permit that Arkan had at the border, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And you personally reviewed it?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally searched the men, the jeeps, after they left the jeeps. Every serial number of every weapon was checked against licences, against the permit, and only then were they allowed to cross. And it was in the presence of another two of my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In your opinion, is there any possibility that the permit was a forgery?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did the permit indicate that Arkan was a member of the JNA, the TO, or the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was just the letterhead of the MUP of Serbia, and in the signature it said "approved by" such and such. If you want me to, I can try to remember before the end of the day and write what this permit looked like. I took that permit away and attached it to my daily reports that I wrote every day and passed it on together with my report. They wanted it as an attachment. I really don't understand why I wasn't given access to the documents I had written before.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did the permit identify Arkan's position in any way, or did it just have his name and the names of his men?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Number one, Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan; number of the pistol and number of the Heckler that he carried. Below that are the names. There was no position indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you call anyone to verify the authenticity of the permit?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I had written in my previous report about the clash, the incident, whatever you want to call it, I also forwarded this report, indicating the exact time and what transpired. And after they left, my superior Zavisic was informed that this person had arrived and he was allowed to cross with such and such a permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Are you aware of any provision of applicable law aside from the permit -- I know you acted on the basis of the permit, but are you aware of any provision of applicable law that would allow a person who was not a member of the army, the Territorial Defence, or the MUP to cross the border between Vojvodina and Croatia in a group of men armed with modern military weapons?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any law enacted on the matter. At that time, there existed federal republic and provincial legislation about procurement and carrying of fire-arms. They were in effect as long as I worked in the MUP, but in that time they changed at least three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is something that wouldn't have happened in peacetime under normal circumstances?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd now like to move on to the incident in which Rade Kostic crossed the border. First of all, just to get the date, you said Arkan crossed the border in July of 1991. Rade Kostic crossed before you left for Eastern Slavonia, obviously, which was in early August. So this was sometime in July or very early August of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After Arkan, came Kostic. I don't know the exact time. That's sometime between me and Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In paragraph 38 of your statement, you said the permit was for Radoslav Kostic and his group. How many people were in the group?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty to 30. Again, everything was checked. Everything was on the permit, all the serial numbers of weapons, just as with the first permit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was: "How many people were in the group?" You said: "Twenty to 30." And then we can wait for the next question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Now we know that -- again, you received the permit, and you acted on the basis of the permit. Were you ever told why Kostic needed to cross the border with a group of 20 to 30 armed men?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you ever learn who these men were?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: From their IDs, I learned that they were from Bosnia-Herzegovina, the area of Ozren, who had family in Borovo Selo. More exactly, in Srepolje [phoen]. Sorry, not Srepolje, Savulja, which is part of Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did this permit say that these individuals were members of the January, the TO, or any MUP?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So, again, am I correct that this situation of a group of 20 to 30 armed men with no affiliation to the JNA, to the TO, or to any MUP is something that not -- would not have happened in peacetime under ordinary circumstances?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why a group of armed men would appear in peacetime anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday, you indicated that you attended the awards ceremony at the Kula camp. Do you know that that camp was named after Rade Kostic?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you see Jovica Stanisic laying a wreath at the memorial to Kostic during the course of the Kula camp celebration?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there during the laying of the wreath, but I was at Kula. I saw it on the video shown me a couple of days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, there's other evidence in this case that indicates that Rade Kostic was a member of the Serbian State Security Service as of the 1st of December, 1990, and that he was deployed to complete different tasks within the State Security Service by Jovica Stanisic on the 21st of June, 1991. Do you have any reason to dispute that information?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of the State Security Service. I can only talk about my three contacts with Mr. Kostic. And I don't know that he was a member of the state security. That's not how he was introduced to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: But you don't have any reason to dispute that information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say neither yes or no. I can only guess. I can only tell you about the occasions where I was present and say what I heard. As for the rest, I can neither confirm nor deny.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: How was Rade Kostic introduced to you?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: As a friend of Ilija Kojic and a man who had worked in the MUP of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: As a close friend of Ilija Kojic?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because he attended the funeral of Ilija Kojic's brother and nephew.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did Kojic and Kostic work together, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, in Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: They knew each other from before the outbreak of the conflict in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: What kind of work did they do together in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Both were members of the ministry; one in public, the other in state security. This is all my speculation. If you want me to lie, I can, but I gave an oath not to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, we definitely don't want you to speculate. Which part of that is speculation, though? You know that they worked together. That's not speculation; correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: My contacts with Kostic were very short. The first time was when he brought that group; the second was at the funeral; and the third and fourth time, again, at funerals. So I really know very little about Mr. Kostic. I can talk for five days about Ilija Kojic. But I don't know anything about Kostic, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You said that you don't know one way or the other whether Kostic was a member of the Serbian State Security Service. Assuming for a moment that the other evidence in this case is correct and that he was, do you know why one of only two people who was allowed to legally cross at your check-point with weapons would be someone associated with the Serbian State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We start with an assumption and then we ask for an explanation, where the witness said that -- Can you answer that question? Do you have any knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Perhaps I can ask it in more general terms, Your Honour. I take your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you know of any reason that individuals associated with the Serbian State Security Service should have special treatment in terms of being able to cross the border between Vojvodina and Croatia with weapons during the period you were at Vajska?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single member of the ministry, either in public or state security, received a permit. Arkan did and Kostic did. Neither of them was a member of the Ministry of the Interior. That was not even written in their permits. If they had been members, I would have been ashamed to be one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: -- you say that you didn't see any members of the DB of Serbia at the crossings. Does this document cause you to revise that evidence in any way?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no members of the DB of Serbia in the area while I was there. Not a single person introduced themselves that way, nor have I ever seen an ID of such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So your conclusion is based on the way people introduced themselves and the IDs that you saw; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Nobody has it written on their forehead that they were an employee of this and that. I reviewed all IDs. I put that on record. I cannot make things up and say that somebody was an employee or not unless they introduced themselves that way or produced an ID showing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to move on to your service in Eastern Slavonia. In paragraph 47 of your statement, you said that you had several conversations with Hadzic and Kojic in which they tried to recruit you to participate in the defence of Eastern Slavonia. As briefly as possible, what did they say to you; what did they want you to do; and why did they want -- well, why was it necessary for you to come?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering they knew I was a graduate of the Military Academy, and I graduated five years before we met, of course, we discussed one another, and that's why I said I could say a lot about Ilija, but as for me personally, I had already met a great number of people who had crossed by that time. I acted in such a way that inspired confidence, and those people in Western Slavonia viewed us as members of the special forces, and in any case, they had a lot of trust in me and my men. And that's why he asked me, I suppose, to cross over. But I didn't do it until my superior contacted me and invited me to cross over together with him. It was only then that I accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you find it strange that they were trying to recruit active policemen, active members, of the MUP to go set up what was fundamentally a military organisation in an area completely outside the jurisdiction of that MUP?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. However, knowing the circumstances, and after talking to my family, my parents, brother, sister, and uncles in Obrovac and Benkovac, I reacted quite differently. I wanted to protect my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you know whether --

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: It's because of my family that I finally left, to protect my sons. I'm a bit emotional when I talk about my family. I hope you don't hold it against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any existing laws and regulations that would provide for members of the Vojvodina SUP and the Serbian MUP to serve in a newly constituted Territorial Defence of a newly constituted autonomous region in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any laws or regulations. All I know is that every tour of ours in the territory of another republic was organised by the federal MUP, federal SUP, be it in Macedonia or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did the federal MUP organise your tour in the Territorial Defence of SBWS?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said this a number of times. Nobody organised my tour. I went as a volunteer on my own initiative. And if I am to be held accountable for that, I'm ready. No state institution has anything to do with my crossing over to that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Well, presumably the Vojvodina SUP had to at least approve it; correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not call or say good-bye to anyone when I was leaving, apart from my superior Zavisic at the time, who crossed over together with me. Except that I brought certificates where I was every month, and I received my salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So the Vojvodina SUP clearly approved of your deployment to the SBWS to the extent that they knew that you were there and they continued to pay your salary. In that sense, they accepted and endorsed that deployment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not deploy me. I crossed over of my own will. I received my salary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. The question was whether they accepted by -- and endorsed any deployment, not necessarily by them, but whomever would have sent you there, by continuing to pay your salary and to accept your absence from duty in your normal position. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said it already. I don't know whether they approved. But I did continue to receive my salary. If the -- the fact that my salary continued to be paid constitutes endorsement, then I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You also indicated you were paid a per diem during your time in Eastern Slavonia. Who paid your per diem?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: We received per diem from Mr. Badza, where a list was made of all of us, 21 of us, if I'm not mistaken, and we all signed for the money we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you know where the money came from?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: All right. We've said that you arrived in Eastern Slavonia in early August and stayed for approximately two months. Were you based in Erdut this whole time?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there the whole time. At the insistence of 16 of us and my insistence and some commanding officers, we were transferred away from Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: When did that happen? How long after you arrived? Obviously an approximation.

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Couple of days before I left Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't quite understand that. You arrived Erdut in early August. How long did you remain in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: About two months. And a couple of days before I left Western Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem, we were transferred away from Erdut. I didn't even manage to move all my things because I was told that my children were alone. I left my things behind and went to rejoin my children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, could I seek clarification on one matter. Earlier you testified - I'm quoting from page 13 - "every month I had to send a certificate in order to be able to receive the salary that Badza had to approve in the -- in the area of Erdut." That suggests that if you could not have shown such a certificate that you might not have received your salary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which - and please tell me whether you agree with that - which means that the services you rendered as a volunteer, if you would have not rendered those services, they would have stopped paying you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the liberation of Dalj, all those volunteers who had worked in Serbia or in the autonomous province in any company could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking about anyone else. I'm asking about your position. If you would not have rendered those services, that they would have stopped paying you, because that was a requirement for receiving your salary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure what you mean when you say "rendering services." What services was I rendering? I don't understand the term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your activities as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just said, all the volunteers who had worked in Serbia and Vojvodina and who had come across with that certificate, we received salary. Which means that without that certificate I would not have been able to receive my salary. And having said that, what I mean to say is that I did not differ in any way from any other volunteer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not interested in whether your position differed that much from others. It's good to know. But I would like to focus on that apparently if you would not have deployed your activities as a volunteer, you would not have been paid by your boss.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that your boss, or the institution you worked for, made payment dependant on your being active as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: A moment ago you told us that a few days before you left the SBWS you were redeployed from Erdut to some other location. What was that other location?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Saponia, very close to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And why did that happen? Was this related to the dispute between Arkan and some of the men you were with?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I and the other 16 members who had arrived insisted, because we didn't want to be close to Arkan or his men. They were not the kind of men we could work with. Not before, not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In paragraph 50 of your statement, you say that Goran Hadzic appointed Badza, you, and the other members of your group to positions in the Territorial Defence. If you know - and you may not - what was Hadzic's legal authority to create a TO and appoint its leadership?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The information about the appointment was conveyed to us by Badza. We received blue IDs containing our names and the title, the function, what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Were those signed by Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: DST-074[Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
